articles.title: In 1865, settlers left rabbits on Enderby Island as food for castaways; 127 years later, the isolated population had developed into a distinct rabbit variety
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Discover the fascinating journey of Enderby Island rabbits, introduced in 1865 as food for castaways, and their evolution into a unique variety facing extinction due to conservation challenges.
articles.body: Rabbits were deliberately released on New Zealand’s remote Enderby Island in October 1865 to provide a potential food source for people who might be shipwrecked in the subantarctic Auckland Islands. The animals were brought from Australia and released in the hope that a breeding population would establish itself. Ultimately, the species survived there for 127 years. They also developed distinctive characteristics after being isolated from the mainland rabbit populations.Enderby Island is the northernmost island of the Auckland Islands group, and it offered an unusually harsh environment for a domestic animal population. The introduced species survived in the cold, wet and windy conditions with no regular management from humans. New Zealand’s Te Ara encyclopedia, using the materials provided by the Department of Conservation, shared that the rabbits were likely descended from British silver-grey rabbits and developed over those 127 years into a distinct population with a silver-grey coat and dark slate-blue undercoat.Due to the isolation, the generations produced looked sufficiently different from ordinary wild rabbits that are found on the mainland. Enderby rabbits are usually moderate-sized animals weighing around 2kg. Most of them had a striking silver-grey appearance. Their heads, ears and tails were relatively darker, sometimes almost black.A rare population turned into an ecological challengeThe isolation that played a role in making the rabbits scientifically and genetically interesting also made them a part of a growing conservation challenge. By the late 20th century, New Zealand authorities were trying to remove introduced mammals from the Auckland Islands because of the effect they had on native vegetation and wildlife. The Enderby rabbits were thus caught between two competing conservation priorities: preserving a genetically distinctive population and restoring an ecosystem from which introduced mammals were removed.A 1995 IUCN report detailed how the rabbits’ extensive burrowing systems were considered a threat to Hooker’s sea lions, as the burrows could potentially trap and suffocate pups. The report detailed how an eradication effort was later executed in 1993, using poison bait followed by hunting over several months. This conservation dilemma was created by the rabbits’ genetic value and the absence of another known wild population of the type.By 1991, estimates suggested that thousands of rabbits remained on the island, and a later review of the eradication programme recorded an estimate of approximately 5,000-6,000 animals at the time. The DOC had reportedly already carried out poison-bait trials in 1991 and 1992 before they decided to proceed with eradication as part of their programme to remove the introduced species from the island.The eradication programme, however, did not allow the distinctive population to disappear completely. The Department of Conservation worked with the Rare Breeds Conservation Society of New Zealand before the eradication began to capture a representative group. In September 1992, 50 rabbits were captured, with 49 surviving the transfer to the mainland. Those animals subsequently became the foundation of a managed breeding population.The rescue before complete eradication The following year, the remaining rabbits on Enderby Island were eradicated. The operation was conducted as part of a bigger effort to restore the Auckland Islands by removing introduced mammals. As per the government records, the eradication operation ran from February to May 1993, and subsequent monitoring completed by February 1994 found no evidence of rabbits remaining on the island or nearby Rose Island.The 1992 capturing of the rabbits therefore meant that the ecological restoration of Enderby did not necessarily put a complete end to the unusual rabbit population. The New Zealand Journal of Ecology notes that breeding groups representing the Enderby rabbits are still maintained in New Zealand. However, their numbers have remained below the level considered necessary to guarantee the breed’s long-term survival.Today, the Enderby Island rabbits survive on the mainland instead of living in the harsh island environment that once isolated and preserved their distinctive genetic legacy. For over thirty years, dedicated breeding programmes have been responsible for breeding programmes are now involved in maintaining the population.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: US and Philippine marines train with BrahMos to deter China
articles.summary: International News: An unusual geopolitical twist just played out in the Indo-Pacific. US and Philippine forces trained together simulating the Brahmos anti-ship missile .
articles.body: An unusual geopolitical twist just played out in the Indo-Pacific. US and Philippine forces trained together simulating the Brahmos anti-ship missile in Exercise MASA 2026, an annual drill between the Philippine Marine Corps and US Marine Corps. What makes this notable is that the Brahmos, the US Naval Institute reported. The Brahmos has jointly developed by India and Russia, this means that American forces are now training alongside a missile Washington has otherwise been trying to steer allies away from, given the ongoing sanctions on Moscow.The drills, held at a remote outpost in northern Luzon last month, practised building a kill chain using drones and ground-based anti-ship missiles against simulated targets. At Manila's northernmost Marine base, planners used Hermes drones to track a surface action group, feeding data to support a BrahMos strike against simulated Chinese warships, including two Type 052D destroyers, a Type 054A frigate and a Type 901 support ship, USNI reported.This fits into a broader US effort to boost long-range strike capability among allies near the South China Sea, following the earlier debut of new American missile systems in northern Philippines near Taiwan. Manila's missileers are now developing tactics for the Brahmos, acquired under a $375 million deal in 2022, marking the first operational use of this missile by any foreign military.At the same time the US Marine Corps is holding a multilateral exercise in Indonesia. The wargame being held in Indonesia is called Exercise Super Garuda Shield, in which according to the Indonesian military, the Indian Army is also participating.India, along with partner nations, is working to keep the sea lanes in the broader Indo-Pacific region secure and free, this at a time when China's growing assertiveness and territorial ambitions have kept tensions on the simmer in the region. “Secure sea lanes, freedom of navigation, respect for international law and unhindered maritime trade are pivotal for collective security & prosperity of the Indian Ocean Region,” stated Raksha Mantri Shri Rajnath Singh, during his visit to Sri Lanka. India is working with regional and global partners to keep the sea lanes open for vessels of all nationalities.

articles.title: In 2019, Seattle residents helped float planted “biobarges” beside a hardened waterway; cameras later recorded young salmon feeding around the new habitat
articles.summary: US News: In a groundbreaking project, Seattle residents collaborated to deploy biobarges that revitalized habitats along the Duwamish River, enabling young salmon to thrive in previously barren waterways.
articles.body: According to NOAA's Lower Duwamish River hazardous-waste site summary, the river once had extensive tidal marshes and mudflats along its banks before channelization and filling transformed much of the estuary into an industrial waterway. Dredging, channeling and a century of industrial activity have destroyed 97 percent of the tidal wetlands that once lined the riverbanks, according to a University of Washington-led study on the Duwamish Floating Wetlands Project. According to the project background for the Duwamish Floating Wetlands Project, along the first seven miles of the Duwamish River, 40 to 60 percent of the linear shoreline is bulkhead, and 50 to 80 percent is riprap. That hardened shoreline leaves young salmon migrating from fresh to salt water with little cover from predators or access to food.Four biobarges, each holding four planted biofilters, were deployedThe team of scientists, headed by Green Futures Lab in collaboration with the Port of Seattle, King County and volunteers from the community, designed four platforms known as Biobarges that were used during a two-year pilot and not as a permanent installation. Each biobarge held four floating wetlands, called Biofilters, planted with native species sturdy enough for scientists to take measurements from.The biobarges were towed into place at two Duwamish sites in April 2019In April 2019, Biobarges were launched into the river and placed within the Duwamish Estuary at two sites. Two of the biobarges were positioned at a heavily industrialized site downriver, while the other two were placed farther upriver in a more vegetated stretch of the river, allowing researchers to compare fish use across a hardened site and a more natural one, according to a University of Washington graduate student's account in the SMEA Currents blog. Monitoring continued through the out-migration season and ran until July 2019, marking the first year of a two-year proof-of-concept pilot project. The structures were then monitored again in 2020, according to the Green Futures Lab website.Local volunteers trained as community scientists carried out much of the fieldwork. They counted and identified juvenile salmon near the Biobarges and at separate reference and control sites without floating wetlands. They also set up and collected the GoPro cameras that recorded underwater footage at each structure. In the project's second year, the volunteers reviewed hundreds of hours of video to identify and count the fish captured on camera, as documented in the study.Underwater footage shows salmon using the structures The rationale for the concept is pretty straightforward. The Green Futures Lab's project background page notes that out-migrating juvenile salmonids rely on a diet of benthic aquatic invertebrates, such as nereid worms and gammarid amphipods, and terrestrial invertebrates, including chironomids, aphids, and tethinids, which are typically produced by vegetation in healthy tidal marshes. Because the bank is reinforced with riprap and lacks vegetation, the Biofilters are intended to attract those insects and invertebrates.Indeed, the footage taken by the GoPro cameras shows juvenile fish, particularly Chinook, swimming around the Biobarges rather than avoiding them. This early observation hints that the floating platforms may be functioning as intended, offering fish a place to linger and feed in a stretch of river where hardened banks and the loss of natural shoreline otherwise limit such opportunities, though the project describes itself as a proof-of-concept pilot rather than a confirmed result. Seattle residents did more than watch the project; they helped assemble the platforms, plant vegetation and observe fish behavior. articles.title: In 1895, a naturalist built a bark-covered cabin in the New York woods to escape visitors and write in solitude; after his death, it became the heart of a 170-acre wildlife sanctuary
articles.summary: US News: Explore the legacy of John Burroughs' Slabsides cabin, a serene retreat in the New York woods that became a 170-acre wildlife sanctuary after his passing.
articles.body: John Burroughs had become popular enough by 1895, and visitors were disrupting the quiet he needed to write. His answer was a small cabin in the woods near his West Park, New York, home. Burroughs built Slabsides that year with help from his son and a carpenter, and used rough wooden slabs with their bark still attached for the exterior walls. The cabin sat on a wooded tract about a mile from Riverby, which was the home where Burroughs lived with his family. The naturalist used the retreat for writing, farming and observation, and it eventually became the physical center of a much larger nature sanctuary that now covers about 170 acres.The cabin was built as an escapeBurroughs was already an established nature writer when Slabsides went up, with his books having made him one of the best-known American writers on the natural world, and the attention brought visitors to Riverby. The Hudson River Valley Institute's historical account says Slabsides served several purposes, but one was to give Burroughs a place away from the steady stream of people arriving at Riverby. He also used the property for farming, cultivating celery in a reclaimed swamp beside the cabin.The name came from the cabin's construction, and its outside walls were covered with rough slabs of wood that still carried their bark. Inside, it had an open main room, a partitioned sleeping area and a fireplace. Burroughs made some of the furniture himself, and much of the interior has survived.Visitors of the cabin included naturalist John Muir, President Theodore Roosevelt and industrialist Henry Ford. Burroughs wrote several works at Slabsides, and used the surrounding woods as both a workplace and a source of material for his nature writing.Nine acres became 170Burroughs and his son developed about nine acres around the cabin, and after Burroughs died in 1921, the property passed to the John Burroughs Association, which had been established to preserve his work and legacy. Supporters raised money to acquire additional parcels as logging and development threatened nearby woodland in the 1960s.Today, the John Burroughs Sanctuary encompasses about 170 acres, with Slabsides at its center. The surrounding property contains woodland and hiking trails rather than the development that Burroughs had sought to avoid when he first built the cabin. The cabin itself received federal recognition in 1968, when it was designated a National Historic Landmark. The landscape is now maintained for both conservation and public access, and the sanctuary grounds are open year-round, while access to the cabin is more limited.Slabsides remains largely intactThe Library of Congress holds photographs of Burroughs at Riverby and Slabsides that were taken between 1915 and 1922. Its catalog says the collection includes images of the naturalist, his family and visitors at the cabin and lists the photographs as having no known restrictions on publication.The sanctuary's trails run through the woods that Burroughs used for walking and observation, while the cabin preserves the setting in which he wrote. The additional acreage was acquired specifically to keep the woods around the cabin from being broken up as development expanded, which makes the 170-acre sanctuary considerably different from the nine-acre tract on which Burroughs originally built his retreat. The property is still maintained by the John Burroughs Association, and is available for hiking, while the cabin is opened on selected occasions and special tours rather than operating as a conventional daily museum.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1999, James Cameron bought a 102-acre California ranch for $4.4 million. 24 years later, the $33 million estate revealed a life far beyond Hollywood
articles.summary: US News: James Cameron bought his 102-acre California ranch in 1999 for about $4.4 million, creating a private retreat far removed from Hollywood's usual celeb.
articles.body: James Cameron bought his 102-acre California ranch in 1999 for about $4.4 million, creating a private retreat far removed from Hollywood's usual celebrity lifestyle. Set within the secluded Hollister Ranch on Santa Barbara County's Gaviota Coast, the property became a family home, writing retreat, working farm and base for the filmmaker's interest in deep-sea exploration and robotics. Over the next two decades, Cameron and his family transformed the estate while preserving its rural character, adding extensive gardens, renewable energy systems, animal facilities and specialised workspaces. When the ranch was listed for $33 million in 2023, its value reflected not just the house, but the unusual life built across its 102 acres.Inside James Cameron’s 102-acre California coastal ranchAccording to a Forbes report, the property sits inside Hollister Ranch, a large private coastal community in Santa Barbara County established in 1971. The wider ranch covers about 14,400 acres, with roughly 8.5 miles of coastline and 136 parcels. Development has remained tightly controlled, with each parcel generally spanning around 100 acres and only a small portion available for residential construction.The main house, built in the 1980s by Hollister Ranch builder Bob Curtis, had about 8,000 square feet of living space when the couple bought it. “It feels rural, but it’s also quite bold, architecturally. It’s very comfortable. It’s not precious,” said James.The interiors reflected the couple's taste for Balinese and Indonesian furnishings. The primary bedroom, for instance, incorporated Balinese fabric and oak flooring, while the great room contained an enormous stone head of Dionysus that Cameron said had come from the façade of a New York hotel.The ranch that became Cameron’s private workshopThe ranch was not simply somewhere the filmmaker went between productions. It became a place where some of his writing took shape.Cameron used the upper library in the main house as a retreat while working on the scripts for Avatar and later films in the series. A separate 2,000-square-foot guest house, positioned higher on the property, also gave him a secluded place to work.For long stretches, he could simply disappear from the usual demands of film production. The isolation suited the kind of concentrated writing he needed to do, particularly as the Avatar projects expanded into multiple films.The property's connection to Cameron's work extended beyond screenwriting. One of the ranch's two barns became a practical workspace for his interest in deep-sea exploration and robotics. The larger barn measures about 24,000 square feet. Cameron said he had kept helicopters there and used the building while developing submarines and robotic equipment for expeditions. Those projects included his extensive work connected with the wreck of the Titanic and his 2012 solo descent into the Mariana Trench.The house was designed for family life, while the surrounding buildings could accommodate equipment associated with some of Cameron's more technically demanding projects.The ranch was built to produce its own power, water and foodThere was also a practical side to the couple's approach to the ranch. The property was equipped to operate off-grid, using solar and wind power. Cameron said the system had extensive battery storage and was capable of supporting the property's roughly 100-kilowatt system for extended periods.Water and food were part of the same arrangement. A well supplied irrigation, while domestic water came through the Santa Anita Mutual Water Company. The garden covered about three-quarters of an acre and contained roughly 150 different crops.It was large enough to become a genuine source of food rather than simply an ornamental garden. Cameron estimated that it could provide produce for 40 or 50 people, with the home's pantry offering further storage.The garden also reflected the family's approach to food and agriculture. The Camerons adopted a plant-based diet in 2012 and had developed broader interests in agricultural and environmental practices elsewhere, including farming operations in New Zealand and Saskatchewan.A childhood shaped by animals, beaches and open spaceFor more than two decades, the ranch was also where the Cameron children grew up.The scale of the property meant that childhood there looked rather different from life in a conventional suburban house. There were horses, donkeys, goats and a pig. The children went hiking, explored the coastline and learned about the animals and plants around them.The family could check tide tables, walk down to the beach and explore the coastal environment without having to leave the ranch's wider surroundings. Some of the stories from those years were less predictable. Cameron recalled the children bringing home animals they encountered, including a young bobcat that the family named Rex. After being raised and eventually released into the wild, the bobcat later returned to the area. It also killed the family's turkey.The ranch was large enough to accommodate gatherings, too. Around the time the property was listed, the Camerons had hosted a five-day family reunion involving about 30 relatives.The $33 million sale goes far beyond the main houseThe residence represents only part of what was being offered for $33 million. The property includes an equestrian facility of about 4,795 square feet, complete with paddocks and ranch offices. Caretaker accommodation and four apartments are incorporated into the ranch facilities.There are also two barns, along with a tennis court and a permitted helipad. The arrangement is significant because the land was never simply carved out as a luxury residential compound. Hollister Ranch has retained its agricultural identity, with cattle ranching continuing across much of the broader property.That working landscape sits alongside the coastal setting. From inside the Cameron house, large windows look towards the bluffs and the Pacific. San Miguel Island, the westernmost of California's Channel Islands, can be seen across the water.Whales, dolphins and sea otters are among the wildlife visible from the property.The Gaviota Coast remains unusually undevelopedThe ranch's value is tied not only to what has been built on it but also to what surrounds it.The Gaviota Coast stretches for about 76 miles along Santa Barbara County and contains one of Southern California's largest remaining stretches of undeveloped coastline. Its landscape brings together coastal bluffs, grasslands, scrub, estuaries and intertidal environments.The area also forms part of a wider ecological corridor associated with the Channel Islands. Development along this section of coast has remained comparatively limited, which gives large private parcels a very different character from the more heavily built-up coastal areas farther south.Hollister Ranch itself has a long history of cattle ranching. The land was established as a private community while retaining much of its agricultural landscape, and residents have access to sections of the shoreline.For the Camerons, the natural setting was closely tied to the way the property was used. It was somewhere to work and raise a family, but also somewhere where the surrounding landscape was part of ordinary life.Why the Camerons decided to sellThe decision to list the ranch in 2023 was not presented as a response to a problem with the property. By then, their three children were largely living independently. Cameron's professional commitments had also become spread across several locations. His work on Avatar took him between Los Angeles and Wellington, New Zealand, while upcoming Alita: Battle Angel projects were expected to take him to Austin.Maintaining a large coastal ranch made less practical sense when the family was no longer based there in the same way. The couple said they hoped a future owner with young children might make similar use of the property.A $4.375 million purchase became a $33 million asking priceThe Camerons paid $4.375 million for the ranch in 1999. Twenty-four years later, the asking price had reached $33 million. That represents an increase of $28.625 million in the property's nominal value. Put another way, the 2023 asking price was roughly 7.5 times what the couple paid.The increase cannot simply be attributed to changes made to the house. The property sits in a highly restricted coastal setting where large parcels are scarce, and comparable sales within Hollister Ranch have commanded substantial prices. Around the time Cameron's property was listed, another front-row Hollister Ranch parcel reportedly sold off-market for $32.5 million, setting a then-record price for the community.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: After a 2001 hurricane devastated Belize’s reef, a marine biologist grew surviving coral fragments on homemade steel tables; 92,000 plantings later, live coral cover was reported at about 60%
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Discover how marine biologist Lisa Carne's innovative coral restoration method revived Belize's reefs after Hurricane Iris, restoring coral cover to 60% with community involvement and genetic diversity efforts.
articles.body: A hurricane devastated a shallow coral reef in Belize, leaving large sections of the seafloor covered in rubble. More than two decades later, branching corals have returned to much of the damaged area. One part of that recovery came from a straightforward restoration method: growing coral fragments in underwater nurseries before transplanting them back onto the reef. According to a study published in Drones, Hurricane Iris struck Laughing Bird Caye National Park directly in 2001, severely damaging the reef and reducing live shallow-coral cover to less than 6%. The devastation became the starting point for restoration efforts at the site. After the storm, marine biologist Lisa Carne found living elkhorn coral fragments scattered among seagrass beds, suggesting that damaged reefs could be rebuilt by moving and growing fragments. That observation eventually led to a restoration programme at Laughing Bird Caye. That idea became the foundation of Fragments of Hope, a community-based restoration organisation in Placencia. The group began replenishing the reef in 2006, using fragments of Caribbean acroporid corals, including elkhorn and staghorn corals. Over the years, thousands of pieces were grown in underwater nurseries before being transplanted onto damaged sections of reef.From broken branches to underwater nurseriesThe restoration method was built on techniques that had already been tested elsewhere in the Caribbean. At Laughing Bird Caye, coral fragments were collected from surviving colonies and attached to concrete bases before being placed on underwater nursery tables made from materials such as steel mesh and rebar. The fragments were allowed to grow in the nurseries and were later transplanted onto degraded sections of the reef. This approach was particularly suited to Caribbean Acropora corals, which are branching reef builders capable of reproducing asexually when branches break and develop into new colonies. Their branching structures also create habitat for other reef organisms.The programme also focused on maintaining genetic diversity by propagating different coral genotypes rather than relying on a small number of colonies. Researchers monitored factors including coral growth, survival, bleaching, temperature and reproduction to assess how well the restored corals were performing. According to research published in Limnology and Oceanography, more than 59,000 nursery-grown coral fragments had been planted across more than one hectare of degraded reef at Laughing Bird Caye during the programme's first decade. The researchers therefore assessed restoration through several measures, rather than treating the number of fragments planted as the sole indication of progress.The reef began to recoverLater monitoring provided another view of how the reef was changing. A 2023 study used drone imagery to map a one-hectare section of shallow reef at Laughing Bird Caye and assess changes in coral cover. The study reported that more than 92,000 coral fragments had been planted on the reef by 2023, while live coral cover was around 60%. Between 2019 and 2020, the mapped area occupied by three selected coral species increased from 2,143 to 2,401 square metres. These measurements provided evidence of changes in coral abundance and distribution across the restored reef, complementing the earlier monitoring of individual transplanted colonies.The restoration also depended on people working directly with the reef. Fishers, dive operators, restoration workers and other members of the local community contributed to monitoring and maintaining the programme. Their involvement helped provide the regular labour and local knowledge needed to keep nursery and transplantation work going over many years. The result was a restoration effort that extended beyond individual coral transplants, with long-term monitoring and community participation becoming part of the work.A restored reef facing a new threatThe recovery at Laughing Bird Caye has not removed the pressures affecting Caribbean coral reefs. Restored colonies still face rising sea temperatures, coral disease, pollution, coastal development and increasingly severe marine heatwaves. These pressures can affect both naturally surviving corals and those established through restoration, making long-term monitoring essential. This challenge became particularly clear during the extreme heat of 2024. Fragments of Hope documented widespread bleaching and heat stress among corals in its monitoring records, while continuing to track colonies that showed signs of resilience. The organisation has also focused on documenting differences among coral genotypes, information that could help researchers understand why some colonies withstand environmental stress better than others. Underwater nurseries and transplanted fragments can help rebuild damaged reefs, but they cannot remove the environmental pressures that caused the original decline.Therefore, Laughing Bird Caye offers a more complicated lesson than a simple restoration success story. Years of nursery work, transplantation, monitoring and community involvement helped increase coral cover across a reef that had suffered severe damage. But the persistence of that recovery will depend on whether the surrounding marine environment remains suitable for corals to survive, grow and reproduce. The restoration can rebuild part of the reef; protecting that recovery requires conditions that allow it to endure.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 2017, a 16-year-old Polynesian surfer began growing coral fragments in underwater nurseries; his team later reported planting more than 221,000 corals across three countries
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Explore how a 16-year-old Polynesian surfer initiated a groundbreaking coral restoration project, resulting in the planting of over 221,000 corals across three countries, and learn about the impact of coral gardening on marine ecosystems.
articles.body: At just 16, a Polynesian surfer looked beneath the waves and saw a reef in trouble. Instead of simply watching corals disappear, he began collecting broken pieces, growing them in underwater nurseries and returning them to the sea. What started in 2017 as a small experiment in French Polynesia has since grown into an international coral restoration effort, with more than 221,000 corals reportedly planted across French Polynesia, Fiji and Thailand.According to UNESCO, Titouan Bernicot grew up on Moorea, French Polynesia, where he witnessed the gradual decline of the coral reefs around the island and became involved in reef conservation as a teenager. He founded Coral Gardeners in 2017 to help restore Moorea's damaged reefs. The organisation's approach involves collecting fragments from resilient corals, growing them in underwater nurseries and later transplanting mature corals onto degraded reef areas.From a surfer's idea to an underwater nurseryBernicot’s method drew on a restoration approach known as coral gardening. In this method, fragments taken from living coral colonies are grown in nurseries until they are large enough to be transplanted onto damaged reef areas. Many reef-building corals can reproduce through fragmentation, allowing broken pieces to survive and develop into new colonies under suitable conditions. Coral Gardeners adapted this approach in Mo'orea, beginning with small underwater nurseries before expanding its restoration work. The organisation now reports that its teams have planted more than 221,000 corals across French Polynesia, Fiji and Thailand.According to a global review published in PLOS One, coral gardening is one of the widely used approaches to active coral restoration. The review found that nursery-grown corals can survive and grow after transplantation, although results vary with coral species, nursery conditions, reef location and environmental pressures. The findings also show why growing corals in nurseries is not, by itself, a guarantee of long-term recovery: transplanted colonies must survive after being returned to the reef and cope with the conditions there.The science behind growing more resilient reefsCoral planting is only one part of restoration. A fragment that survives in a nursery must still cope with waves, predators, disease, warmer water and competition after it is returned to the reef. For this reason, restoration efforts increasingly focus not only on producing more corals, but also on identifying colonies that may be better able to withstand environmental stress. Coral Gardeners has incorporated this idea by collecting fragments from coral colonies that have survived difficult conditions and using them in its nurseries.Research on coral restoration also shows why survival after transplantation matters as much as the number of corals initially planted. A study in Restoration Ecology found that the survival of transplanted staghorn corals varied with factors such as colony size, location, habitat and the year of transplantation. The findings suggest that restoration outcomes depend on where and how corals are grown and planted, rather than simply on the number of fragments produced. This has encouraged greater attention to monitoring coral growth, disease, bleaching and survival after transplantation. Coral Gardeners has also adopted cameras and digital tools to track individual corals and document changes at restoration sites, reflecting a broader shift towards measuring how well restored corals persist over time.A race against a warming oceanHowever, the biggest limitation of the young conservationist’s work is that coral restoration cannot remove the pressures driving coral degradation. The growing threat is marine heatwaves, which cause corals to expel the microscopic algae that provide them with energy and colour. The consequences of coral bleaching can be fatal. Diseases, pollution, destruction of coastal areas, and mechanical damage are also contributing factors to these pressures. Eventually, even coral that is raised in the nursery will face the same problem of warming as wild colonies do.The goal of coral gardening is more ambitious than simply placing coral on the seabed. In order for the restoration to be successful, the final result should be coral colonies that are able to reproduce and rebuild the reef. For Bernicot and other members of Coral Gardeners, this nursery under the water surface becomes a tool instead of a goal. In this way, growing coral can help degraded reefs recover, while selecting colonies that are resilient to harsh conditions may help protect corals from extinction.While the project will not be able to reverse ocean warming or stave off the next marine heatwave on its own, it is an example of what can be accomplished when local communities, scientists, and environmental organisations combine their efforts to implement a relatively straightforward restoration method. What began in 2017 with a 16-year-old surfer examining a damaged reef has become a larger test of whether humans can restore a coral ecosystem before further damage sets in.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Quote of the day by Osho: "The real question is not whether life exists after death. The real question is…" - life lesson behind his words on being truly alive before death
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Osho's thought-provoking words shift attention away from one of humanity's oldest questions and toward something considerably more immediate. \"The rea.
articles.body: Osho's thought-provoking words shift attention away from one of humanity's oldest questions and toward something considerably more immediate. "The real question is not whether life exists after death," he said. "The real question is whether you are alive before death." This exact line is extremely widely and consistently attributed to him across dozens of independent collections of his talks, though given that he delivered thousands of recorded lectures over several decades, later compiled into hundreds of separate books, no single dated source has been pinned down as its original moment. People have spent centuries wondering what genuinely happens after death, and this quote asks something considerably closer to home instead, whether we are genuinely experiencing the life we are actually living right now, or simply moving through a routine of work and expectation without ever really noticing it, checking one more notification before the current moment has even properly ended.Quote of the day by Osho"The real question is not whether life exists after death. The real question is whether you are alive before death"What is the meaning behind Osho's quoteThe quote asks people to reconsider what being genuinely "alive" actually means. In the simplest sense, being alive means being physically present. Osho is using the word in a considerably deeper sense here, describing something closer to being genuinely aware of your surroundings, actually experiencing emotion fully, and making conscious choices rather than simply following an automatic routine. The first sentence acknowledges the real uncertainty surrounding life after death, a question different religions and philosophies have genuinely answered in very different ways. Rather than settling that debate, Osho redirects attention toward a different question entirely, whether we are actually making full use of the life we already have in front of us right now.Why this Osho’s quote still genuinely matters todayThe pressure to stay constantly productive has become a genuinely major part of modern life. Many people measure their day by how much they managed to accomplish rather than by how much they actually experienced while doing it. Technology can make this considerably more complicated too, since a smartphone keeps people connected to work and social media almost constantly, and someone can genuinely sit with family while mentally scrolling through an entirely different world on a screen. Being genuinely busy is not necessarily the same thing as being actually engaged with life. Osho's message does not ask people to abandon ambition or responsibility. It simply encourages them to ask whether the pursuit of those things is genuinely leaving any real room for awareness and enjoyment alongside it.Existing is genuinely not the same as livingThere is a real difference between simply going through the motions and actually feeling connected to your own life. A person may wake up, go to work, return home, scroll through a phone and go to sleep, only to repeat the exact same cycle the next day. Nothing is necessarily wrong with a routine on its own, but if every single day feels genuinely automatic, it can become genuinely difficult to remember when you last actually stopped to experience anything consciously. Living fully was never about being happy every single moment either, since life naturally includes real stress, disappointment and uncertainty too. Being alive in this deeper sense can also mean genuinely allowing yourself to actually experience a difficult emotion, rather than constantly distracting yourself away from it.Stop genuinely postponing lifeIt is genuinely easy to assume happiness will only begin after a particular achievement finally arrives. There is always another goal waiting just past it though. Enjoying the present does not mean abandoning a real future plan. It simply means not sacrificing the entire present moment for a genuinely uncertain future one.Be genuinely present in ordinary momentsA conversation with a friend or a simple family meal can seem fairly insignificant on its own. These moments genuinely make up much of everyday life though, and giving them your full, real attention can actually change how they feel entirely.Question your automatic routinesRoutines are genuinely useful, yet occasionally asking whether they still actually serve you can be genuinely worthwhile. If every day genuinely looks the same, it may be worth actually making room for something different.Do not measure life only through productivityNot every genuinely worthwhile activity produces a measurable result. Resting, spending real time with people you love, or simply sitting quietly may never increase productivity on paper, yet they can still make an actual life considerably richer underneath.Other memorable quotes by Osho"Be realistic: Plan for a miracle.""Life begins where fear ends.""Creativity is the greatest rebellion in existence.""Truth is not to be found outside. No teacher, no scripture can give it to you. It is inside you and if you wish to attain it, seek your own company. Be with yourself."How to apply Osho's quote in daily lifeLiving more consciously does not genuinely require a dramatic lifestyle change. It can start with simply giving full attention to one ordinary activity each day, a breakfast, a conversation, or a short walk without checking a phone. Instead of thinking ahead to the next task, the goal is simply focusing on whatever is actually happening in that exact moment. It also helps to genuinely notice how often you postpone something that actually matters, perhaps a call to an old friend kept waiting for a quieter week that never seems to arrive. It is worth paying real attention to the people physically around you too, since being present with someone while mentally distracted elsewhere is genuinely not the same as actually sharing that moment with them. Finally, allow yourself to enjoy something without needing it to be productive at all, reading a book purely because you enjoy it, or taking a walk without turning it into a fitness target.Final takeaway from Osho’s quote of the dayOsho's quote brings real focus back to a question that is genuinely easier to ignore than any question about death itself, whether we are actually living the life we already have. Nobody can know exactly what genuinely lies beyond death, and people hold deeply different beliefs about it. The present, though, is the one part of life we can actually experience directly for ourselves. The quote works less as an answer about death, and considerably more as a genuine reminder about life. It encourages people to stop treating the present as a waiting room for some future moment, since ambition and long-term plans should never completely replace the actual experience of simply being here now.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: China planted three types of forests on the Loess Plateau; 18 years later, natural forests held 8% more soil moisture
articles.summary: China News: China’s long-running effort to restore the degraded Loess Plateau has revealed a difference between forests planted by people and those allowed to reg.
articles.body: China’s long-running effort to restore the degraded Loess Plateau has revealed a difference between forests planted by people and those allowed to regenerate naturally. Researchers spent 18 years monitoring four forest types in the region, comparing plantations of Pinus tabuliformis, Platycladus orientalis and Robinia pseudoacacia with a natural secondary forest. The results showed that the natural forest had 8% higher soil moisture than the planted forests, while recording greater macroporosity and stronger water movement through the soil. Its soil held more water after rainfall, with average soil water storage reaching around 6 mm, compared with 3–4 mm in the planted forests. Over the 2006–2024 monitoring period, the natural forest consistently maintained higher soil water content, while Robinia pseudoacacia and Platycladus orientalis showed declining moisture trends. The researchers also found that natural forest soils had lower bulk density and higher levels of soil organic carbon and total nitrogen.Natural forests held 8% more soil moistureAccording to the study published in Water Resources Research, titled ‘Natural Forests Accelerate Soil Hydrological Processes and Enhance Water-Holding Capacities Compared to Planted Forests After Long-Term Restoration’, natural secondary forests had 8% higher soil moisture than the planted forests. They also had 68.7% greater macroporosity, a 13.7% larger mean equivalent pore diameter and 34.2% higher saturated hydraulic conductivity. The researchers also recorded higher soil organic carbon, field capacity and available water content in the natural forests.The difference was also visible across the 18-year monitoring period. Natural secondary forests consistently maintained higher soil water content, with peak values reaching 0.28 cm³ per cm³, particularly after substantial rainfall. Pinus tabuliformis showed a slight increase in soil moisture over the period, reaching 0.24 cm³ per cm³, while Robinia pseudoacacia and Platycladus orientalis showed declining soil moisture trends, with average values between 0.15 and 0.22 cm³ per cm³.How did natural forests improve soil water storageThe researchers found clear differences in soil structure between the forests. Natural secondary forest soils had the highest macroporosity and better-connected pores. Their mean macroporosity was 0.113 mm³ per mm³, compared with 0.089 for Robinia pseudoacacia, 0.065 for Platycladus orientalis and 0.047 for Pinus tabuliformis.The natural forests also showed faster soil-water processes during rainfall. Average soil water storage was around 6 mm in the secondary forests, compared with 3–4 mm in the planted forests. The researchers linked this greater storage to the natural forests’ higher macroporosity and pore connectivity, which allowed rainfall to be redistributed and infiltrate the soil more efficiently.Why did natural forests retain more soil moistureSoil moisture in Pinus tabuliformis and Robinia pseudoacacia dropped substantially during the driest period from June to August. In the upper 60 cm of soil, moisture fell. Platycladus orientalis retained more water in deeper layers, but moisture still declined in the upper soil. The secondary forest maintained higher and more stable moisture, particularly in the upper 60 cm.The researchers also found that the secondary forest had lower bulk density, at about 1.0 g per cm³, in the three planted forests. Its soils also contained generally higher levels of total nitrogen and soil organic carbon. The study’s analysis identified soil properties such as bulk density and organic carbon, together with understory plant diversity, as important factors associated with soil hydrological processes and water-holding capacity.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1883, Hawaii successfully introduced African Guinea grass for livestock feed; 143 years later, the 9-foot invasive grass can produce 9,000 seeds per plant and has a 0.89 fire-risk score
articles.summary: US News: What was once introduced as a useful pasture grass has become part of Hawaii's growing invasive-species and wildfire challenge. Guinea grass, a perenn.
articles.body: What was once introduced as a useful pasture grass has become part of Hawaii's growing invasive-species and wildfire challenge. Guinea grass, a perennial species native to Africa, was brought to Hawaii during the 19th century because of its value as livestock forage. Over time, however, the grass spread beyond managed pastures and became naturalised across the islands. Today, its ability to grow into dense stands, produce thousands of seeds and rapidly recover after fire has made it a significant concern for land managers. A historical study, “From the Pasture to the Present: The History of Grass Introductions in Hawai‘i,” documents a successful introduction of Guinea grass by Judge McCully in 1883, with the grass reportedly first planted at a plantation in Kaʻū, Hawaiʻi. The study also records that by 1901, Guinea grass was widely used by the livestock industry. The Hawaii Invasive Species Council now lists the species as a high-risk invasive grass and gives it a 0.89 weed fire-risk score.From livestock forage to an established grassGuinea grass, scientifically known as Megathyrsus maximus, was valued because it grows vigorously and provides forage for livestock. Its introduction was part of a much broader effort to bring non-native pasture grasses to Hawaii as ranchers and agriculturalists looked for plants capable of supporting growing livestock operations. Historical records show that interest in Guinea grass increased during the 1880s. An 1883 account promoted the grass as a potentially valuable forage plant, and attempts were made to obtain seed from the U.S. Department of Agriculture. A successful introduction followed later that year. The grass subsequently became established in the islands. By 1901, contemporary accounts described it as being cultivated successfully by dairymen, while ranchers regarded it as a useful livestock grass. Further introductions continued in the decades that followed, including 192 Guinea grass accessions imported for pasture research between 1911 and 1964.A grass that can reach 9 feetThe characteristics that made Guinea grass attractive as forage also help explain its ability to spread. According to the Hawaii Invasive Species Council, the perennial grass can grow up to 9 feet tall, with leaves reaching about 3 feet long. It can form dense bunches and is capable of growing in a range of environments across Hawaii. Its reproductive capacity is particularly notable. A single plant can produce up to 9,000 seeds, giving established populations substantial potential to expand. The seeds can be dispersed by wind as well as through animal droppings. The species can also reproduce asexually through apomixis, meaning local populations can be genetically uniform. The grass is now naturalised and common on all of Hawaii's main islands, occurring from sea level to about 850 metres in elevation.Why Guinea grass increases wildfire riskThe biggest concern today is not simply that Guinea grass occupies land. Its dense growth can also change how fire moves across the landscape. The Hawaii Invasive Species Council assigns Guinea grass a weed fire-risk score of 0.89, indicating that it is likely to pose a high fire risk in Hawaii. The species can create dense stands in unmanaged areas, particularly when grazing or other forms of vegetation management are absent. During drought, the dry vegetation can provide additional fuel for fires.This creates a difficult cycle. Guinea grass can increase the amount of available fuel, while fire can also create conditions that favour its continued spread. The species is capable of regenerating rapidly after a fire and expanding into burned areas. That gives it an advantage over vegetation that may recover more slowly. Once established, new growth can occupy areas opened by fire, potentially reinforcing the presence of the grass in the landscape.An unintended legacy of pasture improvementGuinea grass is an example of how a species introduced for an economic purpose can have consequences far beyond its original use. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, improving livestock forage was an important agricultural goal in Hawaii. Guinea grass offered exactly the qualities ranchers wanted: vigorous growth, substantial biomass and usefulness as animal feed. But those same characteristics helped the species persist and spread after it moved beyond cultivated pasture. The historical study notes that Guinea grass continued to be introduced for pasture purposes long after the initial 1883 introduction. Today, the challenge is managing a plant that remains useful as forage but can also become invasive when left unmanaged. The Hawaii Invasive Species Council describes the species as having strong allelopathic activity, forming dense stands and increasing fire risk in unmanaged or drought-affected landscapes.More than a century after Guinea grass was deliberately brought to Hawaii as livestock feed, its legacy illustrates the long-term ecological consequences that can accompany the movement of plants between continents. What began as an attempt to improve pasture has left Hawaii managing a highly adaptable grass capable of growing 9 feet tall, producing thousands of seeds and helping create conditions favourable to wildfire.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: An Idaho bridge sat unused for 56 years after mining cut off its road; in 2025, it reopened for wildlife, where nearly 75 animals had been struck within two miles in a decade
articles.summary: US News: In 1969, a bridge over Interstate 90 and the South Fork Coeur d'Alene River near Osburn, Idaho, was built. For more than half a century, the bridge sa.
articles.body: In 1969, a bridge over Interstate 90 and the South Fork Coeur d'Alene River near Osburn, Idaho, was built. For more than half a century, the bridge sat there in the sun, with not much use. The bridge was meant to serve a growing town. But the mining companies bought the land on the far side, blocked expansion and even demolished half the structure. And the bridge ended up being a slab of concrete that carried no vehicles and served no purpose.Carl Wilson, a resident and truck driver who spent more time on Idaho highways than anywhere else, thought about this structure. Driving past roadkill day after day, Wilson began to wonder if that dead-end bridge might have a second life.He had watched local elk and deer herds, and other animals, take their chances with semi-trucks and passenger vehicles. The stretch of I-90 near Osburn ranked second-highest in wildlife collision rates on the interstate between Coeur d'Alene and the Montana border. In the past decade alone, nearly 75 animals were struck within two miles of that single bridge. So Wilson asked himself: what if this bridge could save the animals he watched die trying to cross the freeway? He was sure the old overpass could help. He just needed to convince everyone else. And he did!Abandoned overpass gets a second lifeThe man wasn't the one building roads or taking up conservation projects. He was a truck driver who witnessed what the animals crossing the freeway went through. So he began working the phones, attending meetings, talking to neighbours and state officials about retrofitting the abandoned bridge into a wildlife crossing. Converting an existing structure into something useful sounded good in theory. However, making it possible was harder. But he kept pushing anyway. He gathered community leaders, brought in conservationists and reached out to the Idaho Department of Fish and Game. Slowly, the idea started moving. The Department of Fish and Game teamed up with the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation and several local conservation groups, and decided to make it work. The state officials began working with Osburn residents to secure grant funding and install infrastructure so that the animals could safely cross the interstate via the abandoned bridge. But Wilson didn't live to see it completed. He died in December 2022 at 80 years old, more than two years before the project finished.“He came to me in, like, 2008, when it was just a twinkle in his eye. It just lit a fire under him. It's good to see his dream, that he worked on so hard for all those years, come to fruition,” Kip McGilvery, who has served as the mayor of Osburn for 12 years, told The Spokesman-Review.The Idaho Transportation Department provided crucial support by granting the necessary permits and also helping connect the group with funding resources. Some key staff members in District 1, including former Assistant District Engineer Marvin Fenn and Program Manager Robert Beachler, were instrumental in helping guide the effort to fruition, ITD said in a release.“This project really showcases how creative thinking and collaboration can make use of existing infrastructure in new ways. It was great to see local initiative and partnerships come together to improve safety for both wildlife and drivers,” Beachler said.The new bridge was officially launched in the summer of 2025. Trail cameras mounted on the bridge and nearby underpass recorded what state officials and conservationists had hoped for: deer using the crossing regularly. The footage showed animals taking the bridge route instead of risking the interstate. The fencing did its job, funnel-fencing animals towards the safer crossing. The underpass likewise showed traffic.The bridge, however, does not have a long future. Its life is limited. However, ITD said it's happy to support the community in putting it to good use for now. As the bridge is not used for transportation purposes and is owned by ITD, it is scheduled for removal in 2032, as it ages. “Even temporary or short-term solutions can have meaningful benefits. This project reflects the kind of local collaboration and problem-solving we appreciate being a part of,” District Engineer Damon Allen said. For now, the animals can safely cross the bridge without risking their lives.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.body: At least 25 people were killed after a fire broke out on a foreign-flagged cargo ship undergoing maintenance at a shipyard in China’s eastern port city of Qingdao, according to Chinese state media.The fire erupted at around 11:15 am local time on Thursday at the Beihai Shipbuilding Co. yard in Qingdao, Shandong province, Xinhua reported. Chinese authorities launched an urgent search and rescue operation following the incident."A foreign cargo ship of Beihai Shipbuilding Co., Ltd. in Qingdao, Shandong Province, caught fire during its port call for maintenance, causing heavy casualties," Xinhua said.The agency did not initially provide details on the cause of the fire or the circumstances surrounding the deaths. Some people were also feared trapped or missing on board.Chinese President Xi Jinping called for an urgent search for missing people and accountability for those responsible. Xinhua said he "stressed the need to urgently search for missing persons... and strictly hold those responsible to account".Premier Li Qiang called for the rescue of "trapped" people and urged authorities to ensure injured people received medical treatment. He also called on officials to "strictly prevent secondary disasters".Xinhua published a photograph showing a large vessel docked at a shipyard with several fire engines positioned nearby. The vessel appeared to be the Ocean Melody, a 190-metre bulk carrier sailing under the Liberian flag, according to MarineTraffic, which showed it moored in Qingdao.Xi orders safety checks after fireXi also said that "all regions and relevant departments must draw profound lessons from this incident, thoroughly investigate and rectify all types of fire hazards".The incident comes amid a series of major industrial accidents in China in recent months, raising renewed concerns over workplace safety.In August, an explosion and subsequent fire at a shipyard in Fujian province killed one fire and rescue worker and injured 12 others, state media reported.China launched a campaign targeting fire hazards in high-rise buildings last November, following a major blaze that engulfed several tower blocks in Hong Kong and killed 168 people.A blast at a fireworks factory in central China in May killed 37 people, while a fire at a shoe factory in eastern Fujian province in July killed at least 28 people.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Space-based surveillance: Dhruva to get key systems worth €5m from Safran
articles.summary: India News: BENGALURU: French firm Safran Space, under contracts worth more than €5 million, will supply critical systems, including optical payloads, for satelli.
articles.body: BENGALURU: French firm Safran Space, under contracts worth more than €5 million, will supply critical systems, including optical payloads, for satellites being built as part of India’s Space-Based Surveillance-3 (SBS-3) programme by Dhruva Space, a release from the French President’s Office has confirmed.The contracts, signed during the International Space Summit in Paris, cover communication systems, inertial navigation units, optical payloads and ground stations for the constellation, which is planned to be deployed between 2027 and 2030.SBS-3, a strategic project approved by the Cabinet Committee on Security, will comprise 52 satellites in low Earth and geostationary orbits and is aimed at providing the armed forces with persistent surveillance, secure communications and greater situational awareness across India’s land and maritime areas of interest.The programme marks an expansion of the private sector’s role in India’s strategic space capabilities. Of the 52 satellites, 31 are to be built by private industry, with the remaining 21 being built by Isro. The private-sector allocation has been divided among three companies: Antaris will build 15 satellites, while Pixxel and Dhruva Space will build eight each.Dhruva’s eight satellites therefore form part of the private-sector component of the larger SBS-3 constellation, rather than a separate constellation. The programme is expected to improve the frequency with which strategic areas can be observed and strengthen India’s ability to monitor developments along its borders and across the Indian Ocean Region.The Safran contracts will give Dhruva access to a range of French technologies for the satellites and associated ground infrastructure. Safran said the cooperation illustrates the rise of Indian New Space and the ability of French industry to support the development of India’s sovereign space capabilities. The company also said the partnership could open the way to further cooperation under future phases of the SBS programme.The Paris summit also produced two other India-related announcements. French launch-services provider RIDE! signed an agreement to launch two satellites for TakeMeToSpace, an Indian company developing orbital data centres. The deal builds on RIDE!’s collaboration with Indian space companies, including the launch of a European atmospheric re-entry capsule aboard Isro’s PSLV.Separately, French Earth-observation company U-Space and Indian company Axiscades signed a commercial cooperation agreement to explore the Indian microsatellite market, addressing both commercial and institutional demand.Together, the three announcements point to a widening India-France space relationship spanning strategic surveillance, satellite launches and commercial satellite manufacturing, with Indian private companies increasingly at the centre of the cooperation.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.body: Pakistan appears to have taken a step back from its strong warning to the Houthis a day earlier, with Islamabad on Thursday saying that no military response under the newly signed Mecca defence pact is currently being discussed. The comments came despite its defence minister warning that the agreement could become operational if the Yemen conflict spilled into Saudi Arabia.“There is no such thing under discussion right now ... When time comes (we) will act under the agreement,” Pakistan foreign ministry spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan said on Thursday, referring to the pact signed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye last month.The apparent shift comes a day after defence minister Khawaja Asif warned that the pact could become operational if the Yemen conflict spilled into Saudi Arabia. He said Pakistan was “bound by the terms and conditions of this pact” and would honour its commitments if required.Asif had also warned the Houthis that if they tried to extend the Yemen conflict into Saudi Arabia, “the clauses of this pact over confronting aggression will become operative”. At the same time, he stressed that the agreement was defensive and did not authorise the three countries to independently launch offensive operations against another country.The latest clarification comes as Houthi attacks on Saudi cities and energy infrastructure have intensified.The Mecca joint defence agreement was signed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye on August 7 in Mecca to strengthen collective deterrence and defence cooperation. Under the agreement, “any armed attack against any one of the three States shall be regarded as an attack against them all.” The pact also calls for enhanced defence cooperation among the three countries.No plans to expand Mecca pactPakistan also ruled out any immediate expansion of the Mecca defence alliance, with foreign ministry spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan saying “there are no plans to expand the Mecca alliance.”The clarification comes after earlier discussions about potentially bringing other countries into the arrangement. articles.title: Two beavers were unexpectedly released in Cornwall; six months later, they have built a dam that is reshaping the landscape and attracting wildlife
articles.summary: UK News: Two beavers appeared unexpectedly at Cornwall Wildlife Trust’s Helman Tor nature reserve after six months. Trail cameras have confirmed that the pair .
articles.body: Two beavers appeared unexpectedly at Cornwall Wildlife Trust’s Helman Tor nature reserve after six months. Trail cameras have confirmed that the pair has settled into a territory, with their activity becoming more noticeable as water levels dropped in July. They have built their first dam and begun feeding on leaves and woody vegetation, leaving some trees coppiced or felled in the process. Together, these changes are creating a more varied habitat across the reserve. The new dam has also altered the movement of water, allowing more of it to remain in the area for longer. The altered pools and surrounding vegetation are already attracting other wildlife, including herons and small mammals.How have two beavers shaped Helman Tor after six monthsThe two beavers have established a territory at Helman Tor. The beavers' arrival came unexpectedly, as the animals had been released without authorisation by an unknown third party. Cornwall Wildlife Trust was already exploring the possibility of bringing beavers back to the area and had been considering their reintroduction for several years. Their presence at Helman Tor therefore allowed the trust to monitor the pair closely while continuing to develop its wider plans for beaver reintroduction in Cornwall. Trail camera footage has since confirmed that the two animals are a pair. As water levels fell in July, the cameras captured signs of activity, including the construction of their first dam.How are the beavers transforming their habitatThe beavers have already altered the Helman Tor landscape through feeding and dam building. As the beavers feed on leaves and woody material, some trees have been coppiced or felled across the site. This has created a more complex and dynamic habitat as their woody, leaky dam has changed water movement through the site. The trust says this is particularly beneficial for wetland and wet woodland habitats during hot weather and low flows. The changes demonstrate how the animals can influence vegetation.How has the beaver dam affected wildlife at Helman TorThe new beaver-created pools and dam have become useful to other wildlife as well. Herons are regularly using the pools, while dragonflies skim across their surface. Small mammals have also been seen using the dam to cross the river. Water levels have also risen around the dam. The reserve manager said the team wants to leave the structure in place while the beavers establish their territory and settle into the site. For now, the focus remains on observing how the pair uses the area and how the habitat continues to change as the beavers become significant at Helman Tor.What plans does Cornwall Wildlife Trust have for beaver reintroductionThe unexpected arrival of the two beavers has not changed Cornwall Wildlife Trust’s longer-term plans to reintroduce beavers in Cornwall. The organisation says it will continue its wild release licence application and work with local communities and landowners. Public consultation events are planned across the Par and Fowey catchments. For winter, the trust plans to work with experienced partners such as the Beaver Trust to health-screen the two beavers at Helman Tor. This will become part of the wider preparations for carefully managed and monitored releases in Cornwall. The trust also plans to hold consultation events with local communities and landowners, allowing them to share their views on the proposed reintroduction.How could wider support help beavers return to CornwallThe organisation supports calls for an ambitious beaver reintroduction strategy, funding for farmers and land managers to make more space for water, support for beaver management groups and confirmation that wild beavers can remain in England and Wales. It supports recognising beavers as a native species in Wales and giving them full legal protection. It says these measures would support monitored wild releases. The Helman Tor pair is part of a wider conservation conversation.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: How BJP, Congress turned 80s AI trend turned into an all-out meme war
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: What began as another harmless social media trend, turning present-day photographs into portraits straight out of the 1980s, has now found .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: What began as another harmless social media trend, turning present-day photographs into portraits straight out of the 1980s, has now found its way into the social feeds of politicians has triggered BJP-Congress war of memes.Over the past few days, Instagram and X have been flooded with AI-generated photographs featuring big hair, aviator sunglasses, denim jackets, vintage suits and the grainy finish of old family albums.BJP leaders were among the first to jump onto the trend. Union commerce minister Piyush Goyal shared an AI-generated photograph of himself dressed in a grey suit and aviators, writing simply: "Vibing to the 80s trend."Union minister Kiren Rijiju followed with his own retro look, posing beside a car in an image designed to resemble a photograph from the decade."Why is everyone going back to the 80s vibes? I'm also forced to 80s nostalgia!" he wrote.Congress Sevadal brought Rahul Gandhi into the picture, posting AI-generated photographs of the leader of opposition with the caption: "Rahul Gandhi catches the 80s trend wave."The BJP's official X handle also shared some original pictures of Prime Minister Narendra Modi believed to be from the 1980s era.What started as politicians recreating their younger selves soon became another format for the BJP and Congress to take veiled potshots at each other with AI doing the set design.The Congress's Kerala unit shared an AI-generated image showing a bald man sitting in the front passenger seat of a Maruti Suzuki Omni, with the caption: "A Gujarat street in the 80s."For context, the van, launched in India in the 1980s, became a familiar sight in Bollywood films where it was often shown being used by goons and kidnappers, eventually earning its own "kidnapping van" meme identity.BJP Gujarat hit back with an AI-generated image of its own.BJP's Telangana unit also responded to the Congress post. It shared an image showing a woman in a red dress dancing on a table inside what appeared to be a bar, with liquor bottles visible in cabinets behind her.The description read: "Lusiana, Italy. Circa-1970s."The BJP did not name anyone in the post either, but the reference was widely seen as an allusion to Lusiana, the Italian town where former Congress president Sonia Gandhi was born.Congress MP Shashi Tharoor, however, found a way of joining the trend without asking AI to take him back in time."The 1980s seem to be back, courtesy of AI. I thought I’d join the trend the old-fashioned way," he wrote, sharing photographs that were actually taken during the decade.The pictures included Tharoor with his sons Ishaan and Kanishk.What is the trend?The trend itself is simple. Users upload a present-day selfie to AI tools such as ChatGPT or Google Gemini and ask them to recreate the image as if it had been taken in the 1980s.Unlike a regular vintage filter, the AI rebuilds the photograph around the person’s face, adding everything from big hairstyles and retro clothes to film grain and old-school studio lighting.The result is a polished throwback image that looks straight out of an old photo album or Bollywood publicity still. The trend has spread rapidly across Instagram and X, with influencers, celebrities and now politicians joining in.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.body: Kick streamer Steven “Destiny” has opened up about a frightening experience from his past involving armed people outside his apartment. During a recent Whick TV podcast clip shared on the X, Destiny said several people were outside his home with rifles and asked him questions about his son. The streamer also spoke about being swatted, police coming to his home and his family getting caught up in similar situations. He said these experiences changed how he sees online threats.Destiny recalls armed people asking if his son was inside his apartmentDestiny described one scary incident that he said still feels hard to believe. According to the Kick streamer, a “whole bunch of people” were outside his apartment while pointing rifles at him.He said the people were asking if his son was inside the apartment. He said he has already experienced serious incidents involving his home and family.Kick streamer Destiny says his son and mother were also caught up in the harassmentDestiny also spoke about the first time he said he was swatted. articles.title: ‘My grandpa’s name was Dan Singh’: Fox anchor Alec Nolan hits back at DHS post targeting ‘Mr Singh’
articles.summary: US News: When Fox 7 Austin anchor Alec Nolan saw a US Department of Homeland Security post featuring a South Asian-looking truck driver identified only as “Mr .
articles.body: When Fox 7 Austin anchor Alec Nolan saw a US Department of Homeland Security post featuring a South Asian-looking truck driver identified only as “Mr Singh”, he did not see just another immigration meme. He saw his own family and condemned it.“My grandpa’s name was Dan Singh,” Nolan said in response to the controversial DHS post, recalling how his great-grandfather, Katha Singh, came to the US from India in search of a better life. Katha Singh eventually became a raisin farmer in California, while Nolan’s grandfather went on to work as a truck driver.Nolan called the DHS post “racist and demeaning to anyone with the last name Singh”.The post, shared by the official DHS account on X, used an AI-generated, “Transformers”-style poster as part of the Trump administration’s campaign encouraging undocumented immigrants to leave the US voluntarily.The poster was titled “Transformers: Age of Deportations” and showed a giant Transformer confronting a brown-skinned, bearded man wearing a head covering. Its message read: “America for Americans. Get off our roads; you don't know how to drive, Mr Singh.”The post also encouraged people to report what DHS described as “illegal aliens on American roads” and promoted the administration’s “self-deportation” message.Singh is one of the most widely recognized Sikh surnames and is also deeply embedded in the history of Sikh immigration to the US, with generations of Sikh immigrants building lives in agriculture, trucking, business and other professions.'My middle name is Singh'Michigan Democrat leader Ranjeev Puri called the post vile and said that his middle name is Singh. "As a proud Sikh-American, my middle name is Singh. So are my sons'. It is not a punchline; it is a surname carried proudly by millions of Sikhs worldwide, generations of whom have served this nation, built businesses, and strengthened the fabric of our democracy," Ranjeev said in his statement. "It is xenophobia dressed up as public policy."Who is Alex Nolan?Fox anchor Alex Nolan was born and raised in Fresno and graduated from the University of California, Santa Barbara. His career path was not always in journalism. Before moving into television news, he worked in broadcast sales for KUSA in Denver and KEYT in Santa Barbara.
